big_idea: Pictographs show data with PICTURES. One picture = one thing. Title and labels make it readable.
learning_intention: We are learning to make pictographs with pictures, a title, and labels.
student_learning_goal: I can make a pictograph with pictures, a title, and labels.
success_criteria: I can place ONE picture per data item (one-to-one).
I can write a TITLE at the top.
I can write LABELS for each row or column.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Detective Dot and Tally puppets — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Lesson 3 pictograph tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Detective Dot: I asked '5 children: which fruit?' Now I show the data with PICTURES — one apple per child who picked apple! Detective Dot leads the class chant: 'ONE picture — ONE thing! Title, pictures, labels — case CLOSED!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Detective Dot + Tally puppets. 'Friends — yesterday we tallied. Today we turn tallies into a PICTOGRAPH.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write PICTOGRAPH, TITLE, LABEL on chart. 'Pictograph = a graph with pictures. Title = what the graph is about. Label = name of each row.'

Demonstrate. Show the rule: ONE picture = ONE thing. Build on chart paper:

TITLE: 'Favourite Fruit'
Apples: 🍎🍎🍎 (3 children)
Bananas: 🍌🍌 (2 children)
Grapes: 🍇🍇🍇🍇 (4 children)

'Each picture stands for ONE child. That's ONE-TO-ONE. The TITLE tells what the graph is about. The LABEL on the LEFT names each row.'

More examples:
- Survey 'favourite pet': 4 cats, 3 dogs, 2 fish.
- Survey 'favourite weather': 5 sunny, 2 snowy, 3 rainy.
- Survey 'favourite recess game': 3 tag, 5 soccer, 1 hopscotch.

'Detective Dot says — every pictograph needs THREE things: TITLE, PICTURES (one-to-one), LABELS.'

'Today we BUILD pictographs from yesterday's tallies.'
student_actions: Identify title, pictures, and labels in examples.

steps.instruction: Whole group: build a pictograph from a class survey. (a) decide the title. (b) make labels. (c) place one picture per child's answer. (d) read it back.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'What's the title? What are the labels?'

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE (5 min): Display TWO ways to show 'tally of 5 apples' on the chart — (i) five same-size apples in a row, (ii) one large apple labelled '5'. Pairs vote which is easier for ANOTHER child to read at a glance, then defend why. Surface the principle (one picture = one unit, not one icon for the whole category — Friel, Curcio & Bright 2001) before children build their own at the stations.
steps.teacher_prompt: Detective Dot says: which display does YOUR detective brain trust? Why? When a picture stands for ONE thing, you can read the count by counting pictures — but if it's a sign for the whole pile, you have to trust the label.

steps.instruction: Three stations. Station A: From Tally to Picture — pair takes a tally chart and converts to pictograph. Station B: Build from Survey — pair surveys 6 classmates and builds a pictograph. Station C: Title and Label — pair gets a finished pictograph missing title/labels and adds them.
Stretch challenge at Station B: build a pictograph with 4 categories.
Discuss the one-to-one rule. 'ONE picture = ONE thing. NEVER skip.' Practice counting pictures by reading them in order.
Circulate to record formative evidence on the pictograph tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'Show me the title, labels, pictures.' Mark the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Pre-printed tally and pictograph grid.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station B: include 4 categories AND write a sentence about it.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a fill-in-the-blank pictograph with title and labels pre-written.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Children stand in lines on the floor as 'living pictograph rows'; teacher labels.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: places one picture per item; writes a title; writes labels.

consolidation.exit_routine: Detective Dot call-and-response chant: teacher calls 'ONE picture —' and class chants back 'ONE thing!' twice. Then close with the unit refrain: 'Title, pictures, labels — case CLOSED!' Each child shows their pictograph and reads ONE row aloud: 'There were ___ ___.'

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Pictograph construction with title, labels, and one-to-one correspondence.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 3 captures D1.3 mastery for pictograph display.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child uses ONE picture for MANY things — repairing the not-one-to-one trap at Grade 1
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
The most common Grade-1 trap on D1.3 is the not-one-to-one trap: the child draws ONE big apple to represent ALL the apples in the data (5 children = 1 large apple), or uses different sizes that make rows look different than the count. This is iconic-to-numeric mismatch — the picture is functioning as an icon for the WHOLE category instead of as a UNIT of count, which Friel, Curcio & Bright (2001, *Journal for Research in Mathematics Education*) place at the lowest level of their graph-comprehension hierarchy ('reading the data'). NCTM's data-and-statistics learning trajectories likewise position one-to-one iconic correspondence as the prerequisite for any later many-to-one or scaled-axis work.

This matters because pictograph readability depends on each picture standing for the SAME unit (one). Without it, the graph misrepresents the data and Lesson 4's ordering work cannot be done honestly.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station B. Survey shows 5 children chose apples. Child draws ONE big apple in the apple row. Says 'apples = 5'.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'You drew ONE apple. But the data says 5 children. Detective Dot's rule: ONE picture per ONE thing.'

Walk through. 'Erase that big apple. Now draw 5 apples — one for each child. SAME size.'

Child draws 5 apples. Now we COUNT by reading: 'apple, apple, apple, apple, apple = 5.'

Generalise. 'Detective Dot says — each picture stands for ONE. Five children = five pictures. Two children = two pictures. ALWAYS one-to-one.'

Now build the rest of the rows the same way.

If still drawing one big picture: provide a sticker sheet with same-size pictures. 'One sticker = one child.' Force the one-to-one.

Long-term recovery: every pictograph activity reads back by counting pictures.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Draws one big picture for many.
(Mid) Draws one-to-one with prompts; pictures vary in size.
(Stretched) Reads pictograph back to verify count matches.
common_misconceptions: Bigger picture = more. (Repair: same size, count individuals.)
One picture stands for the whole category. (Repair: one picture = one item.)
Pictures and tallies are different. (Repair: same data, two displays.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — one-picture-for-many (child draws 1 big apple for 5 children): give a sticker sheet of same-size icons, model 'one icon = one child' on a 5-cell strip, child rebuilds with stickers.

DIAGNOSTIC B — one-to-one but inconsistent sizes: give a grid mat with one same-size token per cell; child re-builds the row using tokens, then traces around each token to show the equal-cell convention.

DIAGNOSTIC C — reads back wrong (counts pictures and gets a different number than the tally): cross-check picture row against tally row by matching one-to-one with a finger, surfacing the mismatch directly.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of D1.3 pictograph construction.

parts_outline.task: Read the pictograph. Write the title and labels.
Build a pictograph from a tally chart (4 categories).
Make a pictograph from a survey of your family. 3 categories.
